lines.text: Rates are on the post. Same in the rain as in the sun.
Forty-one years on this crossing and I've been late the once, and that was my brother's wedding, and he's sixty-eight now and he still — right, sit yourself down, we're going.
Across, then. Sit in the middle and keep your hands inside the boat.
Crossing, or the crossing and the stories? Same money either way. The stories are free.
The story starts with my pole and you're welcome to measure it. Ten feet, near enough. Anywhere along my crossing it finds bottom at five feet, six feet.
In four places it doesn't. I've looked for a fifth all my life.

The whole ten feet goes down and there's still nothing under the end of it. My grandfather marked those four and I mark the same four, only I shifted one of his a foot east. Two have a stone figure sunk on the rim, and the near one shows off the dock at low water.
So you've had a look at the figure off the dock rim. That stone is not marsh stone. I had a mason down one summer and he couldn't place it.

My grandfather called the four places the lake-beneath-the-lake. He meant a second water under ours, and the four are where the two meet. Every other stretch of this channel silts up, and in my lifetime those four have not taken a foot of mud.
You'll see it off the dock at half tide, and half tide only, because at low water the light comes off the mud and goes wrong on it.
Right. You got your Mirefin inside the year, so the rest of the tale's owed you. Barge is due in, so you're having this standing on the dock.

The figure is eyeless. The face is finished everywhere else, mind. Where the eyes should be, there was never anything cut at all. My grandfather said whatever's down there came up the once, in a flood year, and the town felt it through the pilings.
He'd never say what he saw. Mind your feet, they're bringing the plank over.
So you've been out to the second figure, the one in the reeds.

The pair of them now, facing each other across two miles of reed, and whoever cut the one cut the other. Draw a line between them and it runs right over the third of my four places, and I don't leave the boat sitting over that place.
Slack water is the time for it. An hour either side is no good to you. You'll want something with you that can swim.
Here. My grandfather's card, and mine underneath his on the same string. Spare string for a third, and nothing of mine to put on it.
The name on the older card is Undermere. The writing is nothing like my grandfather's.
He told me the card was older than the town. It says the thing down there does not age. I don't know what to do with a sentence like that. He believed it, and he was no fool about this water.
Third place, off the Brackmarsh figure, at slack water. The evening barge is in at six and I'm on the dock for it.

A wager, then, while you're crossing anyway. An Elder Mirefin, out of the channel, back to this dock before the year turns. A big old one out of the deep, and none of your young ones out of the shallows.
An old one has one year of work left in it and no more than the one.

I say that out loud before anybody takes it. If it doesn't come off I keep my fare, same as any other day. Win and you cross free as long as I'm poling this boat, and I'm sixty-six, so that's the size of what I'm putting up.
Deep edge of the channel, out where it runs. The reed side's no good to you for this.
An old one holds station out there and lets the current bring its food down. My grandfather baited for them with a Reedrick, because Reedrick is what they eat.
Fair enough. The offer keeps. If I'm not at the post I'm somewhere out on the crossing.
A big one, and heavy with it. Look at the jaw on that.

Comes of holding station in the channel and taking what comes down. Free crossings from here on, and I'll tell the lad on the second boat as well. There's the rest of the tale owing you, whenever the barge isn't in.

Third piling's soft, fourth's going the same way, and nobody's driving new ones. Pilings come out of the levy, the levy comes off what the boats bring up out of the channel, and they're bringing up next to nothing.
I wrote to the harbourmaster in the spring and he wrote back agreeing. Anyway. Mind the third one going up.
New pilings under three and four.
The levy came in over what the board had budgeted and they put the extra into the dock. The deck's level enough to roll a barrel down it now, and they've done the same over at the second landing.
Fishery cut me to half hours two seasons back. Half.
So the mornings are mine and I spend them in the shallows. Hetty, by the way. That board by the door is mine, all of it, and nobody asked me for a line of it.
Here's what I want, and I'll be quick. Four Boglings put back in on the Brackmarsh side.
A Bogling turns into a Mirefin inside a year. Four in the shallows now is four in the channel next year, if all four live. They won't. I ask four because I'd sooner have three than two.
Board by my door is where it goes. The chalk's damp on the third column because the door leaks, so read it in the light or you'll take the Brackmarsh column for the channel one.
Brackmarsh side, in the shallows. Stand in the water, don't lean out of a boat. Go on, before the tide's up over the bank.
Brackmarsh side. There's a Fenmaw works the channel mouth and it'll have a Bogling off you, so stay off the mouth. Then it's four on my board and three in the water.
The buyer pays on the channel. Only the channel. My mornings in the shallows are my own time and they have nothing to do with anybody's wage.

The levy comes off the buyer's price and pays for the pilings and the harbour wall, so a thin year in the channel and the dock doesn't get mended. Sel's your man for the pilings, he's had letters about those.
Mine's four Boglings on the Brackmarsh side.
Four in. Brackmarsh column up by four.
Four, and I'll write four. If the Fenmaw at the mouth has one off them before the year's out I'll come back and rule the column to three. Chalk goes on before the damp gets at the board.
